newsitem.title: ITALY: Ciampi says no plot to keep Italy out of EMU - press.
newsitem.headline: Ciampi says no plot to keep Italy out of EMU - press.

text.p: Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi was quoted as saying on Friday that there was no Franco-German plot to keep Italy out of European monetary union due to the country's high level of public debt.

Ciampi was asked in an interview in the daily La Repubblica whether it was true that the question of Italy's debt mountain was raised by French and German finance ministers at a recent meeting of European Union finance ministers.
"I was there and know the appreciation expressed for Italy's convergence plan...and I heard what the French and German finance ministers said.

"I'd really like to know where this theory of a plot springs from. I'll say this: if we Italians keep on talking about it then at the end of the day somebody will start believing it...self-punishment is a very Italian characteristic," he said.
"No one at the July 7 meeting, either on the French or German side, raised the problem of our public debt," he said in a similar interview in the Turin daily La Stampa.

He said that while some people had said Italy would never make the EMU three percent deficit/gross domestic product goal "and now we're nearly there", the Italian press had now raised the debt question.

Italy's public debt at over 120 percent of GDP was double the Maastricht criterion but was gradually being reduced. "If someone said our public debt is greater than that of Belgium I would tell them to look at the statistics of the two countries," Ciampi told La Repubblica."
"And at the end of 1997 we won't have a lira of foreign debt," he added.

He said that due to the improving public accounts position the Treasury's weight on the markets was less. "The Treasury needs one trillion lire a month less in financing and this is giving fuel to the stock market," which has soared to all-time records in recent days.
Referring to France and Germany's budget difficulties and the possibility of an EMU delay, he noted in La Stampa that the the Maastricht criteria were "simply reference points".
"It is not possible that a major nation can remain outside the Euro for a few tenths of a percentage point," he said.

"The single currency will go ahead as scheduled since a delay would have incalculable damage. And we will do our part to produce a strong euro...The markets already believe in this, why ever shouldn't the Italians?" Ciampi added.
